intro: Janáček wrote this sonata after a worker was killed during demonstrations for a Czech university in Brno. Its second movement builds from a short, returning piano phrase; the interruptions matter as much as the notes.
question: What makes a repeated phrase feel heavier when it returns?

cues.title: A phrase with gaps
cues.text: Listen for short melodic shapes separated by space rather than one uninterrupted tune. On a piano, a held note is already fading; the wait after an attack helps determine the phrase’s length.
cues.evidence: This is an editorial listening guide to the movement’s short gestures. The report shows sparse attacks and low relative level through the opening half-minute.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Outburst and withdrawal
cues.text: The early stretch contrasts forceful playing with a rapid retreat into quiet. Attend to the change in scale within the same instrument, rather than expecting a change of orchestral colour.
cues.evidence: Relative level is high around 0:40–0:45 and markedly lower from 0:50 into the following minute. The broad contrast is measured, not checked by ear.

cues.title: Compare the recurring pattern
cues.text: Across this stretch, compare the pattern of quiet phrases, a stronger outburst and withdrawal with the beginning. Repetition gives you a reference for judging how later passages change their weight.
cues.evidence: The report shows similar pitch collections and level contours around 0:00–0:50 and 1:40–2:30. This suggests recurrence; it does not establish a literal repeat or its precise boundary.

cues.title: A teacher in Brno
cues.text: Janáček helped establish Brno’s Organ School in 1881 and directed it until 1919. Teaching and institution-building occupied decades of his career alongside composition.
cues.evidence: The Leoš Janáček Foundation’s biography documents the school’s establishment and his directorship. https://janacek-nadace.cz/en/zivot-leose-janacka/zivotopis-leose-janacka/

cues.title: The decay between attacks
cues.text: Through the quieter writing, follow the dying sound as carefully as the next attack. A gap between gestures can contain resonance; no new note does not necessarily mean silence.
cues.evidence: The report records quiet, sparsely articulated passages around 2:40–3:15. It cannot distinguish every written rest from the continuation of piano resonance.

cues.title: A longer accumulation
cues.text: In the middle stretch, the piano gathers force over a longer span than the early outbursts. Compare the duration of the build, not just its strongest point.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises substantially from about 3:15 to 4:00, with more detected attacks around 3:45–3:55.

cues.title: The pressure is sustained
cues.text: Across this passage, stronger playing persists instead of withdrawing after one short surge. Compare that extended weight with the brief outbursts near the beginning.
cues.evidence: A sustained high-level region runs approximately 4:35–5:15, unlike the short peaks around 0:40–0:45 and 2:20–2:25.

cues.title: Recognising the shape
cues.text: In the later part of the movement, listen for familiar phrase shapes at a different scale. A return can preserve the sequence of gestures while changing how much force each one carries.
cues.evidence: The report suggests recurring pitch material around 5:25–5:30, at a higher relative level than the opening. A thematic return is a listening hypothesis here, not a verified alignment.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Speech written as music
cues.text: Janáček studied the pitches and rhythms of ordinary speech, attending also to speakers’ expressions and circumstances. His interest was not confined to words: he noted other everyday sounds too.
cues.evidence: The Janáček Foundation biography discusses speech melodies and quotes his account of observing speakers and their surroundings. https://janacek-nadace.cz/en/zivot-leose-janacka/zivotopis-leose-janacka/

cues.title: Fewer attacks, more space
cues.text: Through the final phrases, count the waiting as part of the music. The notes become more widely spaced, and their decay helps determine the pace of the ending.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks are sparse around 7:00–7:20, with lower relative level than in the preceding passages. This does not establish the duration of individual written rests.

cues.title: The remaining resonance
cues.text: Across the close, the remaining piano sound fades rather than leading to another extended flourish. Listen beyond the attacks to the decay they leave behind.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls through approximately 7:20–7:35, with no attacks detected in the last two five-second windows. No final chord is identified from the key estimate.

transitions.title: A quiet ending is made to restart
transitions.how: The first paragraph dwindles through separated piano gestures, then the opening E♭-minor phrase begins again. Janáček reconnects the music by repetition, not by a long modulating bridge. The low foundation and short upper contour recover their original relationship after the intervening harmonic turns. Because each attack is followed by decay, the quiet space before the return belongs to the join: the phrase has to be sounded anew rather than carried across by an unbroken accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: The Opening pattern recurs boundary is 1:42, the strongest novelty peak. The report shows sparse, quiet attacks beforehand; the relations file provisionally matches 2.5–69.5 s with 102.5–169.5 s at a 100 s offset. The repeated opening paragraph and E♭-minor frame are score-informed; the match does not align every rest.

transitions.title: The fragment stops relinquishing its pressure
transitions.how: At the end of the repeated paragraph, Janáček keeps working with short melodic cells instead of introducing a broad second tune. Reiteration, heavier chord attacks and a more insistent lower part make the texture accumulate rather than repeatedly collapse into quiet. The E♭-minor lament has become material for an extended harmonic and registral intensification. Listen for the same compressed, speech-like shapes acquiring weight as their surrounding chords change.
transitions.evidence: The Accumulating force boundary is 3:20; relative level rises from −34.4 dB at 3:15 to −10.5 dB at 3:45, with increased attack density. The score’s short-cell construction supplies the explanation. No specific modulation is inferred from the report’s C♯-minor estimates, and the relations file treats nearby recurrence as local repetition rather than a separate formal return.

transitions.title: The opening survives the central outburst
transitions.how: The extended central pressure gives way to the opening phrase in its E♭-minor surroundings. Janáček does not recover the opening’s fragility immediately: the familiar contour returns with greater weight after the central chordal writing. Recognition depends on the short melodic shape and its low foundation, not on a new tune announcing a new section. The texture then begins to release that weight, restoring the gaps between gestures.
transitions.evidence: The Later return boundary is 5:22, a novelty peak after the sustained 4:35–5:15 high-level region. The relations file provisionally matches 4.5–20.5 s with 326.5–342.5 s, supporting the opening material’s return. The score supplies the thematic identity; the timing remains approximate and the report is not a chord transcription.

transitions.title: The remaining gestures lose their continuation
transitions.how: The returning paragraph continues into a withdrawal rather than another central build. Chordal weight diminishes, the bass leaves more resonance between attacks, and the short upper gestures become increasingly isolated. The eventual E♭-minor triad, E♭–G♭–B♭, closes the tonal frame without turning the lament into major. Janáček makes the ending out of the phrase’s existing gaps and decays; no new closing melody replaces it.
transitions.evidence: The Closing withdrawal boundary is 6:28, a novelty peak; relative level falls across 6:35–6:50 and attacks become sparse later, with final decay at 7:20–7:35. The score supplies the fragmentation and E♭-minor close. The final triad is not inferred from the unreliable last-window key estimates or claimed at 6:28.

composer.background:
Janáček was born in Hukvaldy in 1854, into a Moravian schoolmaster’s family. At eleven he became a chorister at the Augustinian monastery in Old Brno, where Pavel Křížkovský supplied rigorous musical training. His education continued at the Prague Organ School and, more briefly, in Leipzig and Vienna. He returned to Brno to build his career. Teaching, conducting and organising institutions occupied much of his adult life: he founded the Brno Organ School in 1881 and directed it until 1919. The composer now associated with the modernist opera house spent decades preparing other people’s practical musical education.

He married Zdeňka Schulzová in 1881. Their son Vladimír died in childhood; their daughter Olga died in 1903, aged twenty-one. The marriage endured these losses but was repeatedly strained. Friendship with Dvořák and the repertory of Czech choral societies helped shape the earlier compositions, yet Janáček’s mature manner developed slowly. He was already in his forties when the short motives, irregular phrases and repeated accompaniment figures of his later music began to replace more conventional forms. His position in musical history is therefore misleading if determined only by his birth date, a decade before Strauss.
composer.epithet: A Moravian composer who studied the inflections of speech and built operas from short cells, repeated figures and abrupt changes of perspective.
